seo.og_description: What to see and expect in Oujda’s compact, authentic medina – from morning quiet to late-afternoon market energy.

name: Medina of Oujda
hero_subtitle: Eastern Morocco’s living medina: historic gates, spice lanes and everyday life with almost no tourist pressure.

overview.title: A Medina That Still Feels Local
overview.p1: Ask ten people what the Medina of Oujda is and you’ll get answers that all point to the same thing: an authentic, compact quarter where people actually live and work. It sits inside ancient ramparts, entered through monumental gates, and has been the commercial and social heart of the city for centuries.
overview.p2: Go in the morning and the light is soft on the whitewashed walls, the spice sellers are setting up and the alleys feel almost empty. Return in the late afternoon and the energy rises: the call to prayer, the smell of grilled meat, families shopping for the evening meal.
overview.p3: Unlike the famous medinas further west, Oujda’s is rarely overwhelmed by tour groups. You can walk, stop, take photos and talk to shopkeepers without constant pressure. That is its quiet strength.

moods.title: What to Do in the Medina, Hour by Hour
moods.subtitle: The quarter has different faces depending on the time of day. Try to see at least two.

1.title: Quiet, Bright and Easy to Photograph
1.desc: Enter through Bab Sidi Abdelwahab while the shutters are still opening. Walk the spice lanes, look at leather and textile workshops, and enjoy the soft light on the walls without crowds.

2.title: Market Energy and Golden Light
2.desc: From about 4 pm the medina fills with local shoppers. The light turns warm on the stone and the alleys become lively. Ideal for photos and a first taste of street food.

3.title: Grills, Tea and Local Rhythm
3.desc: Some lanes stay active after dark with simple restaurants and cafés. A relaxed way to end the day before heading back to the modern centre or your riad.

food.title: What to Eat Near the Medina
food.p1: You will find simple, good street food rather than tourist menus. Walk a little, look at what locals are ordering, and choose a busy stall.
food.li1: Karan – the famous chickpea gratin, best eaten hot with a glass of barida.
food.li2: Grilled meats and merguez from small street stands.
food.li3: Fresh bread, olives and local cheeses from the market.
food.li4: Snails (babbouche) if you want to try a classic Moroccan street snack.
food.li5: Mint tea or strong coffee in a small café just outside the main gates.
food.p2: Prices are usually posted or easy to ask. Confirm before you order so there are no surprises. If you prefer guidance, a short local food walk is an easy introduction.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Medina of Oujda

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: The medina is in the historic centre. Most taxis know Bab Sidi Abdelwahab. From the train station or modern boulevards it is a short walk or a quick petit-taxi ride.

2.title: Photos and Courtesy
2.desc: People are generally relaxed about photos of streets and architecture. Always ask before photographing individuals, especially women, and respect any refusal.

3.title: Staying Comfortable
3.desc: The medina is compact and safe in daylight. Keep valuables secure, wear comfortable shoes for uneven paving, and carry water in summer. A firm polite ‘no, thank you’ is enough if someone offers unwanted guiding.

q1.question: Is the Medina of Oujda free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. There is no ticket and no gate fee. The medina is open during the day and many lanes stay active into the evening. You only pay for food, drinks or purchases.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit the Medina of Oujda?
q2.answer: Morning for quiet photos and soft light, or late afternoon when the market energy rises and the light turns golden. Avoid the hottest midday hours in summer.

q3.question: Is the Medina of Oujda safe?
q3.answer: Yes for normal daytime and early-evening visits. It is a living residential and commercial quarter. Keep phones and wallets secure and use the same common-sense caution you would in any city centre.

q4.question: How long should I spend in the Medina of Oujda?
q4.answer: Plan 1.5 to 3 hours. That is enough to enter by the main gate, walk the main souks, see the Grande Mosquée exterior and stop for a snack or tea.

q5.question: Is the street food near the Medina safe to eat?
q5.answer: Many visitors eat there without problems. Choose busy stalls where food is cooked in front of you, and be cautious with raw salads or ice if you have a sensitive stomach. Check prices before ordering.
